nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Food fish throughout its range (2523), sold in commercial fisheries throughout Florida, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean (2414; 2323; 2520; 2519).
Recreational:  Excellent recreational food fish (2523; 2323).
Ecological:  Juvenile lane snapper are seasonally abundant, though present throughout the year within ocean inlet seagrass meadows of the Indian River Lagoon and on adjacent shallow ocean reef formations (848, 993, unpubl. data).  Adults are more common on continental shelf reefs between depths of 2 and 60 m, mode of 24 m (2526; 2508; 2323; 848, 993, unpubl. data).  Their year round presence and overall local abundance within the Indian River Lagoon and role as a top predator consuming crustaceans and fishes (2414; 2361; 2522) indicate that lane snapper may influence mortality rates in certain crustacean and fish populations and therefore act as a keystone species in structuring aquatic communities, particularly near ocean inlets.
Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Adults commonly encountered on reef formations and adjacent sand/mud bottom in neritic waters around the Florida peninsula, Bahama Islands and Antilles, Gulf of Mexico to northern South America and to southeastern Brazil (2414; 2523; 2531; 2504; 788).  No significant occurrence north of Florida on the Atlantic coast, but is found throughout the Gulf of Mexico (312; 664; 327; 2323; 2520).
Within Study Area:  Juveniles occur on nearshore ocean reef formations (depths <10 m) and in Indian River Lagoon seagrass and mangrove habitats (848, 993).  As an adult it occurs in ocean inlets and continental shelf reef formations or over adjacent open sand bottom (848).
Life Mode:  A solitary to schooling neritic roving predator (size to 512 mm, 2.27 kg; 2520; 2414; 2523).  Forms predictable aggregations during spawning (2532; 2510).  Highly susceptible to overfishing due to slow growth and longevity in Florida waters (5-6 yrs to reach 300 mm TL and enter fishery: 2520), and presumed low natural mortality as populations of cohorts reach maximum biomass at relatively old ages (6-10 yrs, 2520).
Mobility and Migration: As in other lutjanids, adult lane snapper make limited migrations to spawning sites (2532; 2514).  Pelagic larvae are dispersed via oceanic and continental shelf hydrological factors (2517; 2514).  Juveniles move from coastal and estuarine nursery grounds to deeper (i.e. 4-111 m depths; 2526) estuarine or continental shelf reefs upon maturation (2520).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Larvae: larvae are pelagic, apparently at least proximate to the spawning site over the continental shelf, making nocturnal migrations from near bottom waters to the neuston (2514; 2517).
Juvenile: juvenile Lutjanus synagris associate with inshore and estuarine seagrass meadows and objects rising above the bottom, such as mangrove prop roots or reef formations (581; 664; 2442; 887; 789; 848, 2218, 993).  Newly settled juveniles occur in seagrass meadows within the Indian River Lagoon adjacent to ocean inlets (15+ mm SL at settlement, total seagrass population size range, 15-160 mm SL, n=664; Gilmore unpubl. data 1974-1977; 993) and generally recruit to mangrove prop roots or adjacent shallow rock and coral reef formations as larger juveniles (>160 mm SL; Gilmore unpubl. data).  Christensen (1965) captured 388 juveniles, 18-128 mm SL in seagrass meadows at Jupiter Inlet in the southern terminus of the Indian River Lagoon.  Similar collections have been made elsewhere in Florida: Tampa Bay: Springer and Woodburn (1960), n=17, 18.5-69.1 mm SL; Charlotte Harbor: Wang and Raney, n=361, 16-155mm SL; Cedar Key: Reid (1954), n=32, 21-86 mm SL.
Adult: adults occur over reef and sand/mud bottoms at depths to 111 m (2414; 2526; 848, 993; 2531), extralimital to 400 m (2523).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Juvenile: Newly settled juveniles occur in seagrass meadows and shallow reef formations.
Adult: adults and larger juveniles occur over reef, sand and mud substrates (2414; 2523; 2531; 2519; 993).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: Recorded from salinities of 9.0-47.0 ppt (702; 2515), Indian River Lagoon records, 9.0-38.8 ppt (887; 2515).
Temperature: temperatures of 15.5-32.0 C (581; 887; 2146).  Sensitive to hypothermal stress with mortality observed at 6.0-13.0 C (2146).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic as are most other Lutjanus spp.; oviparous, polygamous, serial, iteroparous, broadcast spawner (2520; 2519; 2514).
Mating/Spawning: Lutjanus synagris and its congener L. griseus have been observed spawning on new and/or full moons in early or late evening in the at specific sites on the continental shelf or near reef formations (2532; 672; 2507; 2524; 2511; 2412; 2514).  Reshetnikov and Claro (1976) reported that L. synagris in Cuba always spawned on a full moon.  Wicklund (1969) made detailed observations of lane snapper spawning in 15 m of water off southeast Florida.  Groups of 5-10 individuals began to interact and leave the main aggregate near the bottom and increase rate of movement about an half hour before sunset.  Multiple dark individuals nudged and chased a lighter individual (presumed to be the female up to 2 m off the bottom at which point all fish became extremely active and swam in all directions depositing eggs and milt in the water column.  Ephemeral color dimorphism has been observed in L. synagris only within spawning aggregations (2532).  Spawning was complete before dark.  Large and small group spawning has been observed most often in the genus with simultaneous broadcast of gametes, dispersing pelagic eggs and larva (2514).  Batch spawning is indicated in Lutjanus spp examined to date (2514).  Recruitment of early juvenile lane snapper, 15-20 mm SL, to the Indian River Lagoon occurs in June, then again from September to December indicating an early spring spawn and then a late summer spawn which may extend into the fall (Gilmore unpubl. data).  Juveniles 15-150 mm SL are present within the lagoon throughout the year (Ibid.) (Gilmore unpubl data).  From 1974 to 1977 the largest single collections of juveniles consistently occurred in October and November indicating the largest spawning period of the year off southeast Florida is summer and fall, the wet season.  Spawning in Trinidad occurs throughout the year though peak spawning was during the spring near the end of the dry season (2519).
Fecundity: Lutjanus synagris fecundities range from 28,750 (29.4 cm TL) to 994,700 (31.0 mm FL-49.4 cm TL) ova per female (2528; 2512; 2511; 2514; 2519).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:   Lutjanus synagris produce 0.65-0.80 mm diameter pelagic eggs with a smooth chorion and unsegmented yolk and single 0.13-0.20 mm colorless oil droplet, which is located on the anterior end of the yolksac in larva (2506; 2517).  Lane snapper eggs hatch in 23 h. at 26 C producing 1.9-2.6 mm yolk sac larva (2506) which exhaust their yolk sac in 3-4 days (2517).
Larvae:  No information specifically on L. synagris, but lutjanids in general have pelagic larval periods which last 25-47 days after hatching (672; 2506; 2509; 2525; 2412; 2517).  Lutjanid larvae are easily recognized by three elongate spines, the 2nd dorsal spine, pelvic spine and preopercular spine (at angle), which are either smooth or with moderately course serrae; and by 15 melanophores on tail at end of yolk sac stage which reduce in number with growth (2517).  It is evident that settlement occurs at least 15 mm SL in L. synagris based on data from collections made in seagrass meadows of the Indian River Lagoon (993; Gilmore 1974-76 unpublished data).  This agrees well with the settlement size of 16-18.5 mm SL for L. synagris specimens taken in seagrass collections elsewhere in Florida (664; 887; 789).
Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 15 mm SL to 85 mm FL - 230 mm TL (2528; 2529, 2530; 2524; 2514; 2519; Gilmore unpubl. data).  The largest individual captured in typical juvenile estuarine habitat, i.e., seagrass meadows, within the Indian River Lagoon was 150 mm SL (Gilmore unpubl. data).
Adults:  Adults may reach 512 mm SL and 10 years of age in Florida, and reach the fishery at 5-6 yrs when obtaining 300 mm TL (2520). However, growth is considerably faster in Trinidad as males and females may reach 300 mm TL in their second year, start maturing at the end of the 1st (males) or 2nd (females) year and support fisheries in their 2nd year (2519).  Longevity is apparently shorter in Trinidad, not exceeding 4 yrs where males grow faster, mature earlier and reach a larger size than females (Ibid.).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: There is no information on the feeding habits of larval lane snapper.  Larvae are presumed to be planktivorous.  Feeding in adult lane snapper occurs throughout the day and night and over a broad depth range, potentially to over 100 m (2361; 2522).  Juvenile and adult L. synagris prey principally on crustaceans from most trophic studies around the Florida peninsula and in the Caribbean (2505; 2440; 2516; 581; 664; 2518; 2528; 2361; Starck 1971; 2527; 2522).  Only one study indicated fishes may contribute a higher percentage than crustaceans in the diet (i.e. 32 to 27 %; 2528).  All studies indicate that L. synagris prey on crustaceans and fish predominately although gastropods, polychaetes and a variety of other benthic invertebrates may also be consumed (2522).  Fishes consumed consisted principally of schooling planktivores (clupeids, engraulids and atherinids) or eels (unidentified), diodontids and ogcocephalids which indicate both benthic and surface feeding (2505; 2440; 2518; 2361).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its diet the lane snapper has the potential to influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range, principally crustaceans.  If snapper populations are reduced by anthropogenic factors it is possible that prey and competitor abundance will be influenced as has been demonstrated in certain fisheries (2513).  Thus, community instability is inherent with the absence of "keystone" species as they influence a wide variety of lower trophic levels.
Factors Influencing Populations:  Recent studies of lane snapper fisheries off the east coast of Florida have indicated that lane snapper did not recruit to the headboat fishery until after age 3 and as of 1984 80% of the maximum yield-per-recruit was being harvested (2520).  Lane snapper from Trinidad commercial fishermen grew faster and matured earlier than those north or south of the Caribbean and therefore, entered the fishery at younger ages than Florida fishes.  Therefore, Trinidad lane snapper and possibly other populations in the Caribbean may support a higher rate of exploitation than Florida populations (2519).

sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic as are most other Lutjanus spp.; oviparous, polygamous, serial, iteroparous, broadcast spawner (2520; 2519; 2514).
Mating/Spawning: Lutjanus synagris and its congener L. griseus have been observed spawning on new and/or full moons in early or late evening in the at specific sites on the continental shelf or near reef formations (2532; 672; 2507; 2524; 2511; 2412; 2514).  Reshetnikov and Claro (1976) reported that L. synagris in Cuba always spawned on a full moon.  Wicklund (1969) made detailed observations of lane snapper spawning in 15 m of water off southeast Florida.  Groups of 5-10 individuals began to interact and leave the main aggregate near the bottom and increase rate of movement about an half hour before sunset.  Multiple dark individuals nudged and chased a lighter individual (presumed to be the female up to 2 m off the bottom at which point all fish became extremely active and swam in all directions depositing eggs and milt in the water column.  Ephemeral color dimorphism has been observed in L. synagris only within spawning aggregations (2532).  Spawning was complete before dark.  Large and small group spawning has been observed most often in the genus with simultaneous broadcast of gametes, dispersing pelagic eggs and larva (2514).  Batch spawning is indicated in Lutjanus spp examined to date (2514).  Recruitment of early juvenile lane snapper, 15-20 mm SL, to the Indian River Lagoon occurs in June, then again from September to December indicating an early spring spawn and then a late summer spawn which may extend into the fall (Gilmore unpubl. data).  Juveniles 15-150 mm SL are present within the lagoon throughout the year (Ibid.) (Gilmore unpubl data).  From 1974 to 1977 the largest single collections of juveniles consistently occurred in October and November indicating the largest spawning period of the year off southeast Florida is summer and fall, the wet season.  Spawning in Trinidad occurs throughout the year though peak spawning was during the spring near the end of the dry season (2519).
Fecundity: Lutjanus synagris fecundities range from 28,750 (29.4 cm TL) to 994,700 (31.0 mm FL-49.4 cm TL) ova per female (2528; 2512; 2511; 2514; 2519).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:   Lutjanus synagris produce 0.65-0.80 mm diameter pelagic eggs with a smooth chorion and unsegmented yolk and single 0.13-0.20 mm colorless oil droplet, which is located on the anterior end of the yolksac in larva (2506; 2517).  Lane snapper eggs hatch in 23 h. at 26 C producing 1.9-2.6 mm yolk sac larva (2506) which exhaust their yolk sac in 3-4 days (2517).
Larvae:  No information specifically on L. synagris, but lutjanids in general have pelagic larval periods which last 25-47 days after hatching (672; 2506; 2509; 2525; 2412; 2517).  Lutjanid larvae are easily recognized by three elongate spines, the 2nd dorsal spine, pelvic spine and preopercular spine (at angle), which are either smooth or with moderately course serrae; and by 15 melanophores on tail at end of yolk sac stage which reduce in number with growth (2517).  It is evident that settlement occurs at least 15 mm SL in L. synagris based on data from collections made in seagrass meadows of the Indian River Lagoon (993; Gilmore 1974-76 unpublished data).  This agrees well with the settlement size of 16-18.5 mm SL for L. synagris specimens taken in seagrass collections elsewhere in Florida (664; 887; 789).
Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 15 mm SL to 85 mm FL - 230 mm TL (2528; 2529, 2530; 2524; 2514; 2519; Gilmore unpubl. data).  The largest individual captured in typical juvenile estuarine habitat, i.e., seagrass meadows, within the Indian River Lagoon was 150 mm SL (Gilmore unpubl. data).
Adults:  Adults may reach 512 mm SL and 10 years of age in Florida, and reach the fishery at 5-6 yrs when obtaining 300 mm TL (2520). However, growth is considerably faster in Trinidad as males and females may reach 300 mm TL in their second year, start maturing at the end of the 1st (males) or 2nd (females) year and support fisheries in their 2nd year (2519).  Longevity is apparently shorter in Trinidad, not exceeding 4 yrs where males grow faster, mature earlier and reach a larger size than females (Ibid.).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: There is no information on the feeding habits of larval lane snapper.  Larvae are presumed to be planktivorous.  Feeding in adult lane snapper occurs throughout the day and night and over a broad depth range, potentially to over 100 m (2361; 2522).  Juvenile and adult L. synagris prey principally on crustaceans from most trophic studies around the Florida peninsula and in the Caribbean (2505; 2440; 2516; 581; 664; 2518; 2528; 2361; Starck 1971; 2527; 2522).  Only one study indicated fishes may contribute a higher percentage than crustaceans in the diet (i.e. 32 to 27 %; 2528).  All studies indicate that L. synagris prey on crustaceans and fish predominately although gastropods, polychaetes and a variety of other benthic invertebrates may also be consumed (2522).  Fishes consumed consisted principally of schooling planktivores (clupeids, engraulids and atherinids) or eels (unidentified), diodontids and ogcocephalids which indicate both benthic and surface feeding (2505; 2440; 2518; 2361).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  Due to its diet the lane snapper has the potential to influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range, principally crustaceans.  If snapper populations are reduced by anthropogenic factors it is possible that prey and competitor abundance will be influenced as has been demonstrated in certain fisheries (2513).  Thus, community instability is inherent with the absence of "keystone" species as they influence a wide variety of lower trophic levels.
Factors Influencing Populations:  Recent studies of lane snapper fisheries off the east coast of Florida have indicated that lane snapper did not recruit to the headboat fishery until after age 3 and as of 1984 80% of the maximum yield-per-recruit was being harvested (2520).  Lane snapper from Trinidad commercial fishermen grew faster and matured earlier than those north or south of the Caribbean and therefore, entered the fishery at younger ages than Florida fishes.  Therefore, Trinidad lane snapper and possibly other populations in the Caribbean may support a higher rate of exploitation than Florida populations (2519).
